bloques.titulo: What you will learn this week

bloques.html:
The final exam covers the whole year: the five weekly tests, plus three punctuation and grammar tools that are new in this guide (section 5). It lasts 40 minutes plus 5 minutes of speaking, and it has seven parts.

Part What you do Where it was taught
1. Listening Listen to a talk twice; answer questions about details, inferences and the main point every week
2. Story Point of view, figurative language, inference, theme, quoting evidence weeks 1 and 3
3. Two texts, one topic Text features, summary, purpose, fact and opinion, comparing texts weeks 2 and 4
4. Poem Metaphor and how stanzas connect week 3
5. Language Verb tenses, comparatives, punctuation, passive voice, roots, complex sentences weeks 1 to 4 and this guide
6. Writing An opinion text with a counterclaim and a rebuttal week 5
7. Speaking Summarize a story, give an opinion with reasons, answer an objection weeks 3 and 5

1. Reading a story (weeks 1 and 3)

  • Point of view. First person: the narrator is a character and says "I". Third person limited: a narrator outside the story reports the thoughts of one character. Third person omniscient: the narrator reports the thoughts of several characters. Test: whose thoughts can you read?
  • Topic and theme. The topic is one or two words (courage). The theme is a full sentence about life that the story shows (Real courage sometimes means admitting a mistake). A theme is not a summary and does not name the characters.
  • Figurative language. A simile compares with like or as. A metaphor says one thing is another. Personification gives human actions to something that is not human. Always ask: what does the comparison make me see or feel?
  • Inference. The text gives clues; you add what you know. A good inference can be proved with words from the text.
  • Evidence. Claim → quote → explain. Copy the exact words inside quotation marks, then say what they show.

2. Reading informational texts (weeks 2 and 4)

  • Text features help you find information: title, headings, bold words, captions, tables.
  • Main idea and summary. A summary gives the main ideas of the whole text in one or two sentences, with no small details and no opinions of your own.
  • Purpose. To inform (encyclopedia, report), to persuade (advertisement, opinion column), to entertain (story), to instruct (recipe, manual).
  • Fact, opinion, reasoned opinion. A fact can be checked and shown to be true or false. An opinion is a judgment (best, beautiful, deserve). A reasoned opinion is a judgment supported by facts.
  • Bias. Ask three questions: Who wrote this? What does the writer gain? What does the text leave out?
  • Two texts, one topic. Use one text to test the other: does a fact in Text A support or weaken a statement in Text B?

3. Argument (week 5)

Claim → reason 1 + evidence → reason 2 + evidence → counterclaim → rebuttal → conclusion. Use formal register: no contractions, no slang. Use modal verbs to be exact: could and may for what is possible, should for a recommendation, must only when you can prove it. Linking words: first, in addition, for example, admittedly, however, therefore, for these reasons.

4. Grammar from weeks 1 to 4

Tool Rule Example
Past simple Regular verbs add -ed; irregular verbs change. Keep one tense in a narrative. climbed, stopped, carried / saw, went, took, froze
Irregular plurals Some nouns do not add -s. child → children, foot → feet, leaf → leaves, sheep → sheep
Comparatives and superlatives Short adjectives: -er, -est. Long adjectives: more, most. Never both. colder, the coldest / more dangerous, the most dangerous
Adverbs Most add -ly. Some keep the same form as the adjective: fast, hard, late. She walked slowly. The wind blew hard. It blew harder.
Complex sentence A subordinate clause (although, because, when, if) + a main clause. If the subordinate clause comes first, put a comma after it. Although it was late, they kept walking.
Relative clause who for people, which or that for things, where for places. The guide, who was a biologist, spoke first.
Roots A root keeps its meaning in many words. spect = look: inspect, spectator / port = carry: transport / astro = star: astronaut

Careful: hardly does not mean "in a hard way". It means "almost not": I could hardly see = I could almost not see. The adverb of hard is hard.

5. Three new tools for the exam

A. The colon (:) before a list. The words before the colon must be a complete sentence.

  • Correct: The climbers carried three things: a rope, a map and a radio.
  • Wrong: The climbers carried: a rope, a map and a radio. ("The climbers carried" is not complete.)

Do not confuse the apostrophe of possession with a plural or a verb: the team's tent (the tent of the team), but the team needed a tent (no apostrophe).

B. Punctuating dialogue. Four rules:

  1. Quotation marks go around the exact words spoken.
  2. The spoken words begin with a capital letter.
  3. If the speech tag (said Carla) comes after the speech, the speech ends with a comma inside the quotation marks. A question mark or exclamation mark stays as it is.
  4. If the speaker goes on with a new sentence after the tag, put a period after the tag and start again with a capital letter.

Model: "The ice is too thin," said Marta. "We should go back."

C. Active and passive voice. In the active voice, the subject does the action. In the passive voice, the subject receives the action. The passive is formed with be + past participle, and the doer may appear after by.

Active Passive
The wind moved the rocks. The rocks were moved by the wind.
Scientists study the ice. The ice is studied by scientists.

Careful: were waiting is not passive. It is the past continuous (be + -ing): the subject is still doing the action. Test for the passive: can you add "by someone" after the verb? The rocks were moved (by the wind) — yes. The researchers were waiting (by someone) — no.

Example 1 — Story. Read this short scene. (Text created for this guide.)

Maya held the last match between two fingers. The wind had already stolen the other three. The fire had to start now, or the night would be very long.

She did not strike it. Instead, she built a wall of stones, small and crooked, on the windy side of the wood. Only then did she kneel.

Question: What is the point of view? Third person limited. The narrator says "she" and reports only what Maya thinks ("the fire had to start now").

Question: "The wind had already stolen the other three." Which device is this, and what is its effect? Personification: the wind "steals" like a thief. It makes the wind seem like an enemy that Maya must outthink.

Question: State a theme. A good answer: Patience and preparation matter more than speed. A weak answer: Maya builds a wall and lights a fire. (That is a summary.)

Question: How do you know Maya is careful? Quote. Claim: Maya thinks before she acts. Quote: "She did not strike it. Instead, she built a wall of stones." Explain: she protects the match from the wind before she uses it.

Example 2 — Two texts. (Texts created for this guide.)

Text A (science magazine): Electric scooters produce no exhaust in the street. However, making their batteries requires mining, and a shared scooter often lasts less than two years.

Text B (scooter company): Our scooters are 100% clean. Smart people have already switched. Join them today!

Question: Which statement in Text B could be checked? "Our scooters are 100% clean" can be checked, and Text A gives a reason to doubt it: the batteries require mining. "Smart people have already switched" is flattery, not a fact.

Question: Which text is more reliable, and why? Give two reasons. Text A. Reason 1: its purpose is to inform, while Text B wants to sell. Reason 2: Text A gives both sides (no exhaust, but mining), while Text B gives only advantages and exaggerates ("100%").

Example 3 — Language.

Punctuate: wait said Maya the wind is changing → "Wait," said Maya. "The wind is changing."

Join with Although: The match was wet. It lit at once. → Although the match was wet, it lit at once. (Comma after the first clause; do not add "but".)

Make it passive: The wind stole the matches. → The matches were stolen by the wind.
A. Story. Use the scene about Maya in Example 1.
Rewrite the first sentence of the scene in the first person, as if Maya were the narrator.
"Only then did she kneel." What does this sentence suggest about Maya's plan? Answer in one sentence.
B. Two texts. Use Text A and Text B about scooters.
Write one fact from Text A.
Write the words in Text B that try to hurry the reader.
A friend says: "Text B must be true because a company would not lie." Write one question about bias that your friend should ask.

C. Poem. Read the poem. (Created for this guide.)

The glacier is a slow white river
that forgot how to run.
It carries boulders on its back
and waits for the sun.
Which line contains a metaphor? Copy it, and say which two things are compared.
Which line contains personification? Copy it.
D. Language.
Write the past simple of these verbs: freeze, carry, see, stop.
Choose the correct words: This is the (most dangerous / dangerousest) road in the region, and trucks drive (slowlier / more slowly) here than anywhere else.
Which sentence uses the colon correctly? (a) She packed: socks, gloves and a hat. (b) She packed three things: socks, gloves and a hat.
Punctuate as dialogue: where is the map asked Leo i left it in the tent
Active or passive? (a) The bridge was built in 1950. (b) The workers were building a bridge.
The root port means "carry". What does portable mean?
Join with Because at the beginning: The ice was thin. The team turned back.
E. Writing and speaking.
Plan an opinion text in five lines (claim, reason 1 + evidence, reason 2 + evidence, counterclaim + rebuttal, conclusion) on this question: Should every student learn to play chess at school?
Say your plan aloud in one minute. Then ask an adult to give you one objection, and answer it.

Challenge mission — The fair advertisement. Text B about scooters breaks the rules of a good argument: it exaggerates, it flatters, and it hides the other side. Your mission: rewrite it as an advertisement that still tries to sell scooters, but in which every statement is true according to Text A. It must have at most 40 words and include one honest disadvantage. Then decide: is your honest version more convincing or less convincing than the original? Write one sentence that explains why. There is no single correct answer; what counts is that a reader could check every statement.
1. I held the last match between two fingers.
1. She had planned to kneel and light the fire only after the wall was ready; she does things in order. (Any answer that shows she prepared first.)
1. "Electric scooters produce no exhaust in the street", or "making their batteries requires mining", or "a shared scooter often lasts less than two years".
1. "Join them today!"
1. For example: What does the company gain if I believe this? or What does the text leave out?
1. "The glacier is a slow white river": a glacier is compared to a river.
1. "that forgot how to run" (a glacier cannot forget), or "It carries boulders on its back", or "and waits for the sun".
1. froze, carried, saw, stopped.
1. most dangerous / more slowly.
1. (b). In (a), "She packed" is not a complete sentence before the colon.
1. "Where is the map?" asked Leo. "I left it in the tent."
1. (a) passive: the bridge received the action. (b) active: past continuous; the workers did the action.
1. Able to be carried; easy to carry.
1. Because the ice was thin, the team turned back.

1. Model: Claim: Every student should learn chess at school. Reason 1: it trains planning; in chess a player must think several moves ahead. Reason 2: it costs little; a board is cheap and needs no field. Counterclaim: some say there is no time in the timetable. Rebuttal: one hour a week could replace part of a free period. Conclusion: for these reasons, chess deserves a place at school. (The opposite claim is equally valid if it has the five parts.)
1. Check with the speaking rubric of week 5: clear claim, two reasons, an answer to the objection, formal language.

Challenge mission, one possible version: Our scooters produce no exhaust in the street. Their batteries do require mining, so we build each scooter to last. Ride one today. (25 words.) Note that "we build each scooter to last" is a promise from the company and cannot be checked in Text A; a stricter version leaves it out.
